 4   A.   My name is Larry Blank. My business address is TAHOEconomics, LLC, 6061

 7   Q.   WHERE ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 8   A.   I am the principal of TAHOEconomics, LLC (“Tahoe”), a Texas-registered consulting

 9        firm I founded in August 1999 (originally in Nevada), specializing in regulatory policy,

10        cost-of-service, rate design, and ratemaking matters involving regulated utility

11        industries.

12   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE A BRIEF SUMMARY OF YOUR BACKGROUND AS IT

13        IS RELEVANT TO THIS TESTIMONY.

14   A.   I have served the public in various capacities for 40 years, including service at the

15        National Regulatory Research Institute (“NRRI”) at Ohio State University and later as

16        the Manager of Regulatory Policy & Market Analysis with the Regulatory Operations

17        Staff of the Nevada Public Utilities Commission. As a consultant, I have served a

18        variety of clients including government agencies, utility customers, and utility

19        companies as an expert witness and/or advisor in over 200 rate cases and rulemakings

20        of various types. My written testimony has been filed before utility regulatory

21        commissions in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Idaho,

22        Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, New

23        York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, and before the Federal

24        Energy Regulatory Commission. At New Mexico State University (“NMSU”), I

 2        Economics, a Master’s in Economics program, and help deliver nationally recognized

 3        rate case training programs, which are attended each year by hundreds of regulatory

 4        professionals from across the United States, promoted by the National Association of

 5        Regulatory Utility Commissioners (“NARUC”). My resume is attached as Exhibit No.

 6        LB-5.

 7   Q.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY TESTIFIED BEFORE THIS COMMISSION?

 8   A.   Yes. I have testified before the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

 9        (“NMPRC” or “Commission”) on multiple occasions.

10   Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING?

11   A.   I am testifying on behalf of the U.S. Department of Defense (“DOD”) and all other

12        Federal Executive Agencies (“FEA”) (collectively, “DOD/FEA”).

13   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE DOD/FEA ELECTRICITY PURCHASES FROM EL

14        PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY (“EPE” OR “COMPANY”).

15   A.   DOD has two major installations receiving electric service from EPE in New Mexico:

16        Holloman Air Force Base (“Holloman AFB”) and White Sands Missile Range

17        (“WSMR”). EPE serves the principal accounts at both installations under Rate No. 10

18        – Military Research and Development Power Service. WSMR receives service under

19        Rate No. 10, Option A, while Holloman AFB receives service under Rate No. 10,

20        Option B. EPE also serves smaller accounts associated with Fort Bliss’s operations in

21        New Mexico, although Fort Bliss receives most of its retail electric service under EPE’s

22        applicable Texas tariffs rather than its New Mexico tariffs.

23                EPE also serves other smaller DOD and FEA facilities, including the Las

24        Cruces VA Clinic, post offices, and other federal facilities under other applicable rate

25        schedules. Accordingly, DOD/FEA’s interests in this proceeding extend beyond Rate


     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank                                                     Page 2
  1        No. 10 and encompass multiple EPE rate classes, depending on the specific facility,

 2        voltage level, usage profile, and applicable tariff.

 3   Q.   HOW DO WSMR AND HOLLOMAN AFB DIFFER FROM OTHER EPE

 4        CUSTOMERS?

 5   A.   WSMR and Holloman AFB differ from other EPE customers in several respects. First,

 6        these facilities receive electric service at higher voltage levels (115 kV) at the

 7        demarcation point, and the cost to operate and maintain the distribution system,

 8        including downstream electric facilities and appurtenances beyond EPE’s demarcation

 9        point, is the responsibility of the installations rather than EPE.

10                Second, Holloman AFB has unique service arrangements with EPE, including

11        an agreement under which Holloman AFB purchases the output of a dedicated 5-

12        megawatt (“MW”), behind-the-meter photovoltaic (“PV”) facility located on

13        government land (“Holloman PV”). The Holloman PV facility is owned and operated

14        by EPE but under the terms of a Power Purchase Agreement (“PPA”), the costs of the

15        facility are borne directly by Holloman AFB. Accordingly, Holloman AFB is

16        responsible for the entirety of the costs associated with the dedicated facility, and costs

17        associated with the solar unit are not allocated to EPE’s other retail customers.

18        However, the efficiency and operation of the EPE-owned and -operated solar facility

19        does impact Holloman’s cost of service. Thus, Rate No. 10 – Option B should be

20        understood as an integrated, customer-specific rate and contractual arrangement

21        designed to recognize, at least in part, the unique economic characteristics associated

22        with the Holloman PV facility.

23   Q.   ARE THERE ANY OTHER DOD/FEA WITNESSES SPONSORING

24        TESTIMONY IN THE CURRENT PROCEEDING?

 3                    II. PURPOSE, SUMMARY, AND RECOMMENDATIONS

 4   Q.       WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

 5   A.       The purpose of my testimony is to evaluate the cost-of-service (“COS”) studies

 6            prepared by EPE, 1 as presented in EPE’s amended filing (“Amended Filing”), 2

 7            supporting testimony and workpapers, and discovery responses supporting the

 8            Company’s request to revise its electric rates and terms of service. 3 In addition, I review

 9            EPE’s proposed allocation of base rate revenues. Specifically, my testimony addresses

10            the following:

11                1. EPE’s revised COS studies, sponsored by EPE witness Mr. Adrian Hernandez
12                   as updated in the Amended Filing; 4

13                2. The allocation factors and supporting load-calculation workpapers used in the
14                   COS studies, as sponsored by EPE witness Ms. Enedina Soto; and

15                3. EPE’s proposed class revenue allocations, and EPE’s proposed large-load
16                   tariffs, Rate No. 50 – High Load Factor Power Service Rate (“Rate No. 50”)
17                   and Rate No. 51 – Large Load Power Service Rate (“Rate No. 51”), supported
18                   by the direct testimony of EPE witnesses Hernandez and Mr. Manuel Carrasco.

 3            A. COS Studies

 4                •   The general structure of EPE’s sponsored COS studies, including the Full Cost

 5                    of Service (“FCOS”); Jurisdictional Cost of Service (“JCOS”); Demand,

 6                    Energy, and Customer Components (“DEC”); and Class Cost of Service

 7                    (“CCOS”) studies, is consistent with generally accepted utility ratemaking

8                     practices. Specifically, EPE follows the traditional embedded cost-of-service

9                     methodology by functionalizing, classifying, and allocating (or directly

10                    assigning) utility costs. 5


11                •   For production plant, EPE proposes to allocate peaking generation using the

12                    Four Coincident Peak (“4CP”) Demand–Production allocator, identified as

13                    D2PROD, and all other production plant using the 4CP-Average and Excess

14                    (“4CP-A&E”) Demand–Production allocator, identified as D1PROD. 6 For

15                    certain production operations and maintenance (“O&M”) costs, including

16                    Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) Account 556 – System

17                    Control and Load Dispatching, EPE proposes to use the Twelve Coincident

18                    Peak, Average and Excess (“12CP-A&E”) allocator, identified as DPROD12. 7

19                    For transmission plant and most transmission O&M costs, EPE proposes to use

20                    the 4CP / D2TRAN allocator, except for FERC Account 561 – Load

 3            •   EPE’s meter data for Rate No. 10B is net of energy generated by the 5-MW

 4                Holloman PV facility. The Holloman PV facility provides an economic benefit

 5                to EPE’s system customers by reducing the energy and demand that otherwise

 6                would be supplied by EPE’s general system resources. However, for the reasons

 7                I provide in Section III.B, I propose to adjust the meter data used by EPE to

 8                reflect normalized production, which in turn produce revised allocation factors.

 9                I have incorporated these revised load adjustments into the DOD/FEA CCOS

10                Study.


11            •   EPE separates FERC Account 370 – Meters into Advanced Metering System

12                (“AMS”) and Non-AMS categories and allocates each category using separate

13                weighted meter allocators. While the use of more granular cost-allocation data

14                is generally appropriate when it produces a reasonable reflection of cost

15                causation, my review of EPE’s proposed allocators indicates that this approach

16                produces a substantial disparity in the resulting per-unit cost assignments. I

17                recommend that the Commission reject EPE’s separate AMS and Non-AMS

18                meter allocators and instead adopt a single combined allocator for meter plant

19                and meter-related O&M expenses. I discuss my proposed treatment in Section

20                III.C. This adjustment provides a more transparent, balanced, and cost-

21                causative allocation of meter costs and has been incorporated into the

22                DOD/FEA CCOS Study.

  1        B. Rate Class Base Revenue Allocation

 2            •   The Company proposes to move all rate classes to full cost-of-service levels

 3                based on the results of its CCOS Study, after crediting non-firm revenues to the

 4                firm rate classes. Although full movement to cost is one approach available to

 5                the Commission, the magnitude and uneven distribution of the proposed

 6                increases support the use of gradualism and rate mitigation to avoid undue rate

 7                shock. For example, under the Company’s CCOS Study, the Rate No. 01 –

 8                Residential Service class would receive a 73.37% increase, while some other

 9                rate classes would receive a decrease.


10                       I propose to use the results of the DOD/FEA CCOS Study to guide the

11                allocation of the approved base-revenue increase, while also applying

12                gradualism and rate mitigation (or rate banding). My proposed base-revenue

13                allocation and associated class increases are presented in Table 1 and are based

14                on a floor and cap approach described in Section V. Under this approach, a rate

15                class with a negative or below-the-floor, cost-based increase would receive an

16                increase equal to half (50%) of the system-average increase, while no rate class

17                would receive an increase greater than 1.35 times the system-average increase.

18                Rate classes with cost-based increases between the floor and cap would receive

19                increases adjusted proportionally, as necessary, so that the resulting class

20                increases recover the overall approved revenue increase after application of the

21                floor and cap. As shown in Table 1, under the $70.724 million firm-class CCOS

22                base-revenue deficiency, which represents a 50.53% system-average increase

23                for firm retail classes, my proposed allocation produces a minimum class

24                increase of 25.27% and a maximum class increase of 68.22%.


     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank                                                      Page 8
  1            •   Given the magnitude of the Company’s proposed increases, EPE proposes to

 2                implement the increases for certain classes in two phases. For phased classes,

 3                EPE applies the same percentage increase sequentially: first from present

 4                revenues to Phase 1 revenues, and then from Phase 1 revenues to the full cost-

 5                of-service revenue requirement. For example, EPE states that the Residential

 6                Service class would receive a 31.6% increase in Phase 1 and a second 31.6%

 7                increase in Phase 2, with the second percentage increase applied to the higher

 8                Phase 1 revenue level. The Company proposes that Phase 1 take effect on

 9                January 1, 2027, with Phase 2 taking effect on October 1, 2027. The Company

10                applies this phase-in treatment to Rate Nos. 01, 05, 10B, 12, 25, and 26.


11            •   I recommend expanding the phase-in treatment to additional classes facing

12                significant increases and extending the period between the effective dates of the

13                Phase 1 and Phase 2 increases from nine months to 12 months. Any rate class

14                with a mitigated increase exceeding 60% of the system-average increase

15                approved in this proceeding should be subject to a phase-in. Based on the

16                Company’s proposed 50.53% system-average increase, this criterion would

17                apply to any class with an increase greater than approximately 30.32%. Under

18                my proposal, these rate classes would receive their approved increase in two

19                phases, 12 months apart. The Phase 1 increase would equal the greater of the

20                equal-sequential percentage increase or an applicable Phase 1 minimum floor

21                of 80% of the phase-in threshold, and Phase 2 would recover the remaining

22                approved increase relative to the Phase 1 revenue level. This approach extends

23                the Company’s phase-in treatment to Rate No. 07 – City and County Service,

24                and Rate No. 10A – Military R&D, Option A, while preserving the Company’s

25                proposed phase-in for Rate Nos. 01, 05, 10B, 12, 25, and 26. The resulting

     Direct Testimony of Larry Blank                                                      Page 9
  1                phase-in provides a more gradual transition for classes receiving relatively large

 2                increases.


 3        C. Rate No. 10A and Rate No. 10B Customer Charges

 4            •   Although EPE’s proposed customer charges for Rate No. 10A and Rate No.

 5                10B are derived on the Company’s CCOS Study results, the proposed increases

 6                are substantial. EPE proposes to increase the Rate No. 10A monthly customer

 7                charge from $220.00 to $3,205.35, an increase of $2,985.35, or approximately

 8                1,357.0%, and to increase the Rate No. 10B customer charge from $220.00 to

 9                $3,119.13, an increase of $2,899.13, or approximately 1,318%. To mitigate

10                these rate impacts, I recommend limiting the customer charges for Rate No.

11                10A and Rate No. 10B to 75% of the cost-based levels approved in this case.

12                For illustration, under the Company’s amended proposed cost-based customer

13                charges, this recommendation would result in customer charges of $2,404.01

14                for Rate No. 10A and $2,339.35 for Rate No. 10B.


15        D. Modifications to EPE’s Proposed Large-Load Tariffs

16            •   EPE’s proposed Rate Nos. 50 and 51 are intended to address the costs and risks

17                associated with new large-load customers. I recommend that the Commission:

18                   o Reject Rate No. 51 as proposed, or, alternatively, increase its minimum-
19                       demand threshold from 10 MW to 25 MW;

20                   o Reduce the minimum Energy Service Agreement (“ESA”) term from 20
21                       years to 10 years;

22                   o Revise the damages provisions to reflect identifiable unrecovered costs
23                       and mitigation; expressly grandfather existing customers and existing
24                       load and prohibit involuntary migration to Rate No. 50 or Rate No. 51;

     With respect to the AMS_METER, NON-AMS_METER, and CUST902 allocators, please
     explain how the value assigned to each rate class was developed. Specifically:

     a.   State whether each class value represents an actual number of meters, a weighted
          number of meters, or another measure;

     b.   If weighting is applied, describe the weighting methodology, identify each weighting
          factor used, and provide the calculations supporting the resulting value for each rate
          class;

     c.   Provide a narrative explanation for the values assigned to each rate class, including a
          specific detailed explanation of the values assigned to Rate No. 10A and Rate No.
          10B;

     d.   Confirm whether the CUST902 allocator and the NON-AMS_METER allocator are
          intended to be identical in EPE’s filed CCOS Study.


RESPONSE:

     Please see objections. Without waiving these objections, El Paso Electric Company
     ("EPE") responds as follows:

  a) Each class value represents a weighted number of meters. As explained in Adrian
     Hernandez’s Amended Direct Testimony at Q106, EPE utilizes two distinct meter
     allocators in the CCOS study: the Non-AMS Weighted Meter Allocator (NON-
     AMS_METER) and the AMS Weighted Meter Allocator (AMS_METER).

  b) EPE develops the AMS_METER and NON-AMS_METER allocators by multiplying each
     rate class’s actual year end meter count by a weighting factor based on EPE’s typical
     installed meter cost relative to the minimum typical installed meter cost within the
                                                                        Docket No. 25-00082-UT

      applicable rate class. Installed costs include meter equipment and installation costs. Please
      see DOD 02-03_Attachment 01, tabs “Meter Allocators - AMS” and “Meter Allocators -
      Non AMS,” for the class-specific weighting factors and supporting calculations.

   c) Each rate class’s meter allocator value reflects the actual year end meter count for that rate
      class, weighted for differences in typical installed metering costs. Please see DOD 02-
      03_Attachment 1 for the supporting detail for each rate class.

      Rate No. 10A has five three-phase, CT-installed non-AMS meters, while Rate No. 10B has
      two. Both rate classes have a typical installed cost per meter of $1,676.11. Dividing this
      cost by the minimum non-AMS installed cost of $204.45 produces a weighting factor of
      8.1981. Accordingly, Rate No. 10A has 40.9905 weighted meters, rounded to 41, and Rate
      No. 10B has 16.3962 weighted meters, rounded to 16. Both rate classes have zero AMS
      meters.
